# kulp-rand-hardware-enabled-governance-mechanisms-2024
- **URL:** https://www.rand.org/pubs/working_papers/WRA3056-1.html (landing page) and https://www.rand.org/content/dam/rand/pubs/working_papers/WRA3000/WRA3056-1/RAND_WRA3056-1.pdf (81-page PDF, text extracted locally) · **Accessed:** 2026-09-16 · **For:** v2→v3 response round, slice N (item N3a)
- **What it establishes:** A leading hardware-governance paper expressly proposes putting hardware-enabled mechanisms ON consumer devices (gaming GPUs, consoles, laptops). This falsifies any unqualified claim that the hardware-governance literature designed its mechanisms "expressly not for the devices people own." Scope caveats: the context is US export control (keeping consumer chips export-exempt); the mechanism proposed for consumer devices is "Fixed Set" (a cap on high-bandwidth communication outside a small pre-authorised pod, to block aggregation into a supercomputer) — not metering or attestation of what an owner computes; and the paper frames it as minimising impact on consumer use.
- **Key passages (printed page; PDF page = printed + 11 in the body, roman numerals in front matter):**
  - p. viii (Exec. summary): HEMs could "reduce the chips' usefulness to develop or run a frontier AI model of national security concern while minimizing the impact on the chips' usefulness for other commercial or consumer applications."
  - p. ix (Exec. summary, Fixed Set): "This approach is particularly useful for further securing consumer devices, such as gaming GPUs and gaming consoles, that are subject to the BIS Notified Advanced Computing License Exemption. Consumer devices could be equipped with Fixed Set mechanisms to prevent their aggregation into a supercomputer for developing large AI systems of concern."
  - p. x (Policy Implications): "HEMs on GPUs could prevent the misuse of consumer chips, reduce chip smuggling, and limit unauthorized actors from using cloud services to access advanced chips." and "HEMs could also help ensure consumer GPUs are not used to create unauthorized supercomputers. ... If such HEMs were incorporated into consumer products, they could obviate the need for additional export controls on consumer GPUs, thereby reducing adverse impacts on consumer products and helping to preserve the current dominant market positions of U.S. GPU makers."
  - p. 7 (PDF p. 18): "Which chips to use HEMs on. HEMs can be utilized on the most-advanced data center chips or on less advanced chips, such as those marketed as consumer devices (but which nonetheless could be misused to develop frontier AI systems)." and "1. HEMs could further secure consumer-grade chips from misuse. The current export controls apply only to chips "marketed or designed for data center use." However, consumer chips can still be used for frontier AI development or inference ... If sufficiently secure, placing HEMs on consumer hardware would allow them to continue to be exempted from export controls while preventing them from being misused."
  - p. 52 (PDF p. 63): "Notably, consumer devices, such as laptops and video game consoles, that only consist of a single CPU and GPU require less outside communication at high speeds and could use this mechanism with limited downsides."
  - p. 57 (PDF p. 68): Fixed Set "could limit all high-speed communication outside a single GPU (for instance, if a chip were sold individually as part of a consumer product, such as a gaming console) to prevent many consumer device-chips from being aggregated into a supercomputer."
  - Also p. 8 (PDF p. 19): Offline Licensing "could tie the usability of chips to rigorous know-your-customer (KYC) checks."
- **Reliability:** Primary. RAND working paper (not peer-reviewed; "intended to share researchers' latest findings and to solicit informal peer review"), written as a comment to BIS on the Oct. 2023 interim final rules.
- **Relevance to this project:** The review's finding is CONFIRMED, with a pinpoint correction: the three quoted sentences are at p. 7, p. ix and p. x respectively (front-matter roman pages plus body p. 7), not a continuous "pp. 7–10." Citation: Gabriel Kulp, Daniel Gonzales, Everett Smith, Lennart Heim, Prateek Puri, Michael J. D. Vermeer, Zev Winkelman, "Hardware-Enabled Governance Mechanisms: Developing Technical Solutions to Exempt Items Otherwise Classified Under Export Control Classification Numbers 3A090 and 4A090," RAND Working Paper WR-A3056-1 (published Jan 18, 2024), doi:10.7249/WRA3056-1, 81 pp.
